title: Statistical Communication & Decision Use
description: Reading and writing statistics for real decisions: honestly communicating uncertainty, spotting p-hacking and base-rate neglect before they mislead a room, and building a defensible recommendation out of evidence that is never perfectly certain.
subject: Business Statistics
audience: Undergraduate & MBA students of Business Statistics and Analytics

topics.title: Reading & Writing Statistics for Managerial Decisions
topics.tagline: A number without its context is not yet information

blocks.text: A slide says "Customer satisfaction: 7.8." Nothing in that sentence tells a manager whether 7.8 is good or bad, how many customers it is based on, or what to do differently tomorrow.

blocks.title: Table 1.1 · What every statistical claim should carry with it
rows: A satisfaction score means something different depending on the scale and question wording
The same average from 20 and from 2,000 respondents carries very different weight
A confidence interval or margin of error, not just a point estimate
7.8 compared to what: last quarter, a competitor, a target?

blocks.text: Compress any finding into **one sentence** an executive could act on: "Satisfaction is 7.8 out of 10, based on 150 responses (likely true value 7.6-8.0), essentially unchanged from last quarter's 7.7."

items.q: Name three things a statistical claim needs besides the number itself.
items.a: Any three of: what was measured and how, the sample size, a measure of uncertainty, a comparison baseline, or the practical implication.

topics.title: Communicating Uncertainty
topics.tagline: Confidence intervals and margin of error: three views of the same honesty

blocks.text: Two surveys both report average satisfaction of 7.8, one from 150 responses and one from 25. As bare numbers they look identical.

n = 150, mean = 7.8, SD = 1.4: standard error = 0.114, 95% CI = (7.57, 8.03).

n = 25, same mean and SD: standard error = 0.280, 95% CI = (7.22, 8.38).

blocks.caption: Same point estimate (7.8), very different precision: the larger sample's margin is less than half as wide

blocks.text: Presenting only the point estimate with the confidence interval buried in an appendix. The width of the interval is often the most decision-relevant piece of information.

items.q: Why is the n=150 interval narrower than the n=25 interval?
items.a: Standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(n), so a larger sample gives a narrower interval around the same estimate.

case_study.title: The Sales Manager Who Fired the Wrong People
case_study.subtitle: Reading Regression to the Mean as a Management Signal

paragraphs.text: A regional sales manager rewards the top 10% of performers and puts the bottom 10% on an improvement plan.
The former top performers fell and the former bottom performers rose, and the manager credited discipline for the rise and blamed rewards for the fall.
Quarter-to-quarter correlation was only about 0.21, so extreme scorers regress toward the mean with no intervention at all.

case_study.discussion: What evidence would have distinguished "the plan worked" from "this is regression to the mean"?

practice.question: Rewrite the slide bullet "Sales are up 12%" as a proper one-sentence statistical claim. What else would you need to know?
practice.answer: Sales rose 12% quarter-over-quarter (based on all transactions, n = ...), against a typical seasonal rise of X%, likely true range Y-Z%. You need the population, a baseline and a measure of uncertainty.

practice.question: Explain what a 95% confidence interval does and does not claim.
practice.answer: It does not claim a 95% probability that the true value lies in this one interval. About 95% of intervals built this way over repeated sampling would contain the true value.

mistakes.title: Reporting a number with no uncertainty
mistakes.text: The interval is often the most decision-relevant part of the finding.

mistakes.title: Crediting an intervention for regression to the mean
mistakes.text: Extreme groups revert on their own when correlation between periods is imperfect.

revision.checklist_title: Questions to ask before presenting any statistic
checklist: Have I included the sample size and a measure of uncertainty?
Can I state the finding, its uncertainty and the action in one sentence?
